name: Probability matching
statement: Asked to guess which of two outcomes comes next, people spread their guesses in proportion to how often each occurs instead of always naming the likelier one.
meaning: The task is a long run of guesses about a random binary sequence with fixed odds. Take the standard 70 to 30 split. Naming the frequent outcome every time is right 70% of the time. Splitting guesses 70 to 30 is right 58% of the time, because 0.7 squared plus 0.3 squared is 0.58, the figure Saldana and colleagues set out. The gap is the cost of the behaviour, and it is why economists have treated the result as a challenge. Arrow, quoted by both Vulkan and by Shanks, Tunney and McCarthy, wrote in 1958 that the individual does not reach the optimal behaviour at any point, even in the limit. Two things travel under the name. One is the strict rule of guessing at exactly the observed rate. The other is the weaker and much more common finding that people choose the better option more often than its base rate but well short of always. The literature calls the second over-matching, and most published group means are cases of it.

origin.who: David A. Grant, Harold W. Hake and John P. Hornseth
origin.note: Their paper is "Acquisition and extinction of a verbal conditioned response with differing percentages of reinforcement", and it is the earliest experiment in Vulkan's survey of repeated binary-choice studies. Vulkan's table records 37 subjects over 60 trials choosing the alternative that was correct 75% of the time on 85% of trials. Those figures are read off Vulkan's table, not off the 1951 paper, which was not obtained. Vulkan also lists an earlier item, Humphreys (1939), in his references without discussing it in the text; that paper was not obtained either, and nothing on this page rests on it.

evidence: Vulkan's survey gathers the group means from the probability learning experiments of the 1950s and 1960s and sorts them by whether money was at stake. Without payment the means sit close to the outcome rate: Neimark and Shuford's 36 subjects chose a 0.67 alternative on 0.63 of trials, and Suppes and Atkinson's 30 subjects chose a 0.60 alternative on 0.59. Payment moves them up. Myers and colleagues in 1963 report 0.75 for a 0.70 alternative unpaid and 0.87 for the same alternative when a correct guess paid one cent. Siegel and Goldstein's groups faced a 0.75 alternative and chose it on 0.75 of trials for nothing, 0.86 for five cents a hit, and 0.95 when a miss also cost five cents. Vulkan's reading of his own tables is that matching is not robust, that it falls as rewards and trials grow, and that group averaging biases the estimate towards it. Edwards's 1000-trial study, which he tabulates per subject, makes the last point concrete: 7 of 80 subjects chose the better side on every one of the last 80 trials, and only 16 of 80 chose it at or below its actual rate. Shanks, Tunney and McCarthy then built the conditions the survey pointed at. Their participants got 5 pence a hit and lost 5 pence a miss, an accuracy score against an optimal algorithm every 50 trials, and up to 1,800 trials. Six of 16 maximised after 300 trials, 8 of 12 after 1,800, and 9 of 12 in the paid group with feedback after 1,500. Pooling the last two gives 71% of participants maximising, with 95% limits of 18 points either side. How the task is described matters, though not in every way. Koehler and James gave one group of 158 students the two strategies in words before playing a ten-guess version of the game, and asked which would win more money. Strict maximising ran at 53% in that group against 35% in the group given no such hint, chi-square 5.14, p = .023. Among the participants who picked maximising as better when asked after the game, the hint lifted maximising from 44% to 69%, chi-square 7.99, p = .005. An earlier manipulation by the same pair did nothing. Telling participants the totals rather than showing them draws one at a time, and asking for a count of guesses rather than a sequence, left the choice index flat, F(1,98) = 0.003 for the learning change and F(1,98) = 0.45 for the test change. Naming the better strategy works. Removing the chance to hunt for patterns does not.

replication.headline: The behaviour survives in the simplest version of the task and disappears from most variants of it, so what replicates depends on which version is run.
replication.detail: Saldana, Claidiere, Fagot and Smith ran four preregistered experiments on 238 adults and 20 Guinea baboons using matched tasks. With two options and a 70 to 30 reward split, only 5 of 20 humans were maximising in the final block of 240 trials, 6 were over-matching, and the other 9 fell in the matching or random range. Doubling the task to 480 trials changed little: 13 of 39 maximising, 8 over-matching, 11 matching, 6 random. With three options and a 70-15-15 split the picture inverts, and 12 of 20 maximise on the short task and 26 of 39 on the long one. Shanks, Tunney and McCarthy reach the opposite headline from the same starting point by loading the binary task with money, feedback and 1,500 trials, and report 71% of participants maximising against Vulkan's survey means that hug the base rate. Both results stand. The disagreement is about which conditions count as the phenomenon.

study.cite: Saldana, C., Claidiere, N., Fagot, J., & Smith, K. (2022). Probability matching is not the default decision making strategy in human and non-human primates. Scientific Reports, 12, 13092.

limits: No meta-analysis of probability matching was located. Crossref, OpenAlex and open-web searches for one returned methodological papers about meta-analysing binary outcomes and nothing on this effect, so no pooled estimate and no interval are given here. The historical group means all come from Vulkan's tables rather than from the papers behind them, and Vulkan warns that the sequences used by Grant and colleagues, Jarvik, Gardner, Anderson and Whalen, and Goodnow were not independent from trial to trial. He records that Fiorina concluded on those grounds that the whole psychological literature on probability matching should be disregarded. One much-cited moderator has failed a direct test. Wolford, Newman, Miller and Wig reported in 2004 that a verbal working-memory load pushed people towards maximising, on 10 per condition. Schulze, James, Koehler and Newell ran a preregistered replication with 162 participants and found the final-block difference between the n-back and control groups at t(109) = -0.562, p = .576, d = -0.107, 95% CI [-0.479, 0.266], with a Bayes factor of 0.232 against the effect. Their control group also gives a clean baseline: 18 of 57 met the 95% criterion for maximising in the final block. West and Stanovich's 2003 paper on cognitive ability, cited throughout this literature, was not obtained, and the cognitive-ability claims here rest on Koehler and James instead.
misreadings: Probability matching is not the matching law. Vulkan opens his survey by separating the two, and puts Herrnstein's law in an appendix of behaviours that do not conflict with reward maximising. Shanks and colleagues make the sharper point that the matching law, through melioration, predicts maximising at asymptote in exactly this task, because the frequent option always has the higher momentary reinforcement rate. The conflation is live: Lo, Marlowe and Zhang open a 2021 PLOS ONE paper by calling probability matching "also known as the 'matching law', or Herrnstein's Law". A second misreading takes group means for individual strategies. Shanks's group curves ran above 0.9 while single participants split into stable maximisers and stable matchers, and Vulkan argues that averaging over a group is biased towards the less extreme hypothesis. The third is the story that animals beat people at this. Saldana and colleagues found their baboons maximising across binary and ternary tasks, but humans matched the baboons on the ternary task, and when the baboons were given a correction procedure that removed the cost of a wrong answer only 2 of 13 still maximised, the rest settling on one spot on the screen. The last misreading is that matchers do not know better. Koehler and James asked their participants to rank the two strategies after playing, and 9 of 21 strict matchers picked maximising as the one with the higher expected return. What separates matchers from maximisers looks like reflection rather than knowledge. Scores on the three-item Cognitive Reflection Test correlated with the number of dominant-colour guesses at r = .40 in their first experiment and r = .36 in the second, and 2 of the 18 participants scoring zero maximised against 17 of the 23 scoring three. Formal training points the other way. Lo, Marlowe and Zhang, reporting on 75 subjects, found that those who had taken probability and statistics classes randomised more, with a logistic coefficient of -0.283 and z = -2.445, which they call the opposite of what they expected.
